stem: A company runs an application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application keeps its data on an unencrypted Amazon EBS data volume. A new security policy requires the company to encrypt this data at rest. The company must also ensure that every new EBS volume that anyone creates in the Region from now on is encrypted. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a snapshot of the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption turned on, and replace the volume with a new volume from the copy.
options.why: [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so you snapshot the volume and [create an encrypted copy of that snapshot](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot) for a new volume.

options.text: Use Elastic Volumes to modify the existing volume in place, and turn on encryption while the volume stays attached to the running instance of the application.
options.why: You [cannot change the encryption status](../facts/kms.md#kms-ebs-encryption-status-fixed-at-create) of an existing volume, so Elastic Volumes offers no setting that encrypts it in place.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and wait for Amazon EBS to encrypt the existing volume in the background.
options.why: Encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), so the existing volume stays unencrypted.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in the Region, and keep the AWS managed key as the default encryption key.
options.why: Encryption by default is a [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region), and it ensures that [all new volumes are always encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) there.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, finds new unencrypted volumes in the Region, and replaces each one with an encrypted copy.
options.why: A scheduled function is code to build and run, and a new volume stays unencrypted until the next run; one [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) covers every new volume.
options.misconception: a custom scheduled job is needed to keep new volumes encrypted

explanation: Two needs decide this question: the existing data and every new volume. The existing data moves to an encrypted volume through an encrypted snapshot copy. Encryption by default then makes the account [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only), with one Region setting and no code.
takeaway: Encrypt an existing volume through an encrypted snapshot copy; for new volumes, use the [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region).
twin: If the stem said "every new volume in two Regions" instead: turn on encryption by default in each Region, because it is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting).
say: The old volume goes through an encrypted snapshot copy, and encryption by default covers every new one.

stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in two AWS Regions, us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Teams in both Regions create new Amazon EBS volumes every day with their own scripts and templates. A new security policy requires that every new EBS volume in these two Regions is encrypted at rest. The company does not want to change the scripts and templates of the teams. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: every new EBS volume in these two Regions

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 only, because the setting then applies to every Region of the account.
options.why: Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so new volumes in eu-west-1 stay unencrypted.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in us-east-1 and in eu-west-1, and keep the AWS managed key of each Region as the default key.
options.why: Encryption by default is a [single setting per region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region) that ensures [all new volumes are always encrypted](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-encryption-by-default-per-region), with no change to the scripts of the teams.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function every hour in each Region that finds unencrypted volumes and turns on encryption for each volume in place.
options.why: [You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encrypt-existing-volume-via-snapshot), so the function has no in-place step, and new volumes stay unencrypted between runs.

options.text: Create a customer managed key in each Region, turn on Amazon EBS encryption by default in both Regions, and set each new key as the default key.
options.why: It works, but you then create and manage two keys, while EBS already has [a unique AWS managed key in each Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-aws-managed-key-alias-per-region).
options.misconception: encryption by default needs a customer managed key

explanation: Two Regions and the least effort decide this question. Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting), so you turn it on in each of the two Regions. After that, the account will [enforce the encryption of the new EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only) that the teams create there, and their scripts stay the same.
takeaway: Encryption by default is [a Region-specific setting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-region-setting): turn it on in every Region where teams create volumes.
twin: If the stem said "the existing volumes must also be encrypted" instead: also replace each one from an encrypted snapshot copy, because encryption by default [has no effect on existing EBS volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-encryption-by-default-new-resources-only).
say: Encryption by default is per Region, so I'd turn it on in both Regions.

stem: A company must keep one Amazon EBS snapshot of a database volume for each month for seven years to meet a compliance rule. The snapshots are kept for long-term storage and are infrequently accessed. When an audit needs an old snapshot, a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable. The company currently keeps all of these monthly snapshots in the standard tier. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to keep these snapshots?
keywords: a restore that takes up to three days is acceptable

options.text: Keep the monthly snapshots in the standard tier, and add a tag to each snapshot that marks it as part of the compliance record.
options.why: It meets the rule, but the archive tier offers [up to 75 percent lower snapshot storage costs](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-75-percent-lower-cost) for rarely accessed snapshots.
options.misconception: the standard tier is the only place to keep an EBS snapshot

options.text: Copy the monthly snapshots into an Amazon S3 bucket through the Amazon S3 API, and store them in the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.
options.why: EBS snapshots are [only available through the Amazon EC2 API](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-snapshots-not-via-s3-api), so the S3 API cannot copy them into a bucket.

options.text: Move each monthly snapshot to the Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive tier after it is created, and restore it from there for an audit.
options.why: AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily) that you keep for a long time and rarely restore.

options.text: Delete every monthly snapshot except the most recent one, because the newest snapshot holds all of the data that the volume needs.
options.why: The newest snapshot restores the volume as it is today, and the compliance rule needs the state of each month.
options.misconception: the latest snapshot holds every earlier state of the volume

explanation: Seven years of monthly snapshots that are rarely restored decide this question. AWS recommends the archive tier for [monthly, quarterly, or yearly snapshots](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-recommended-monthly-not-daily), and its storage costs less than the standard tier. A restore from the archive tier can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours), which the three-day limit allows.
takeaway: Monthly snapshots kept for years and rarely restored belong in the EBS Snapshots Archive tier.
twin: If the stem said "an auditor needs a snapshot within one hour" instead: keep the snapshots in the standard tier, because an archive restore can take [up to 72 hours](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-archive-restore-up-to-72-hours).
say: Monthly snapshots kept for years go to the archive tier.

stem: A company runs a database on one Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on one Amazon EBS volume. The company accepts the loss of up to one day of data and a recovery time of several hours. The company does not run any of its instances across multiple Availability Zones today. The company must be able to recover the database if the whole Region becomes unavailable. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: if the whole Region becomes unavailable
loss of up to one day of data

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume. After a failure, create a volume from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone of the same Region.
options.why: A restore in another zone stays in the same Region, because [snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing), and that whole Region is down.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot of the volume and copy it to a second Region. After a failure, create a volume from the copy there.
options.why: You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt), so a daily copy in a second Region restores the database there within the one-day loss limit.

options.text: Keep the data on the current volume. After a failure, detach the volume and attach it to a new instance in another Availability Zone of the Region.
options.why: The volume and the instance [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance), and the whole Region is down, so the volume cannot be attached anywhere.

options.text: Take a daily snapshot and copy it to a second Region. Keep a standby instance running there, and restore each new copy to its volume.
options.why: It works, but a standby instance that runs every day costs more than a restore after a failure, and several hours of recovery are acceptable.
options.misconception: a database can be recovered only from a standby instance that is already running

explanation: The loss of the whole Region, with one day of data loss allowed, decides this question. [Snapshots are constrained to the Region](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-regional-copy-before-sharing) where they are created, so a backup that must outlive the Region needs a copy in a second Region. You can [copy snapshots from one Region to another](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-copy-cross-region-and-encrypt) each day and restore the latest copy after a failure.
takeaway: A backup that has to outlive a Region needs a snapshot copy in a second Region.
twin: If the stem said "if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable" instead: restore the latest snapshot in another zone, because you can [restore volumes in any Availability Zones](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-restore-in-any-az-of-region) of the Region.
say: If the whole Region can fail, the snapshot needs a copy in a second Region.
